doc.title: Ruthie Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 28, 2023

title: Atlantic Records development deal and learning in New York
summary: She took a songwriting development deal, fulfilled it with legal counsel, kept her songs, and used three years in New York to learn the industry from songwriters.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: It seems that you have a fairly well defined vision for your music and I read this bit about you turning down a deal with Atlantic Records. Is that correct?

I actually did take the deal and I was very careful with how I presented my songs. Because it was really a development deal. It wasn’t necessarily a full on recording deal. And I had great counsel representation, lawyers, who helped me through that contract and understand that contract and be able to fulfill that contract, which was basically they wanted a specific amount of songs written within a specific amount of time and then your contract is over. And I fulfilled that. And so I was able to walk away knowing that I had fulfilled my duties in this contract. Not only that but I could walk away with my own songs.
They hired you as a songwriter then?

Basically hired me as a songwriter with, as a performer in development. In other words if they had chosen any of the songs I had written to record then that would lock me into basically not owning, first of all not owning those songs or the performance, or anything else. A lot of those contracts are really vague about owning the person, their name, their brand and I knew that. So I wrote songs, but I kept a few to myself too. And the songs that I did turn in, none of them really were contracted or basically picked to be recorded. So I recorded on my own.

That little thing you just said reminded me of Nat Adderley, who was contracted to write a tune and he wrote “The Work Song” and he said, “Wait a minute, I’m going to keep this for myself and I’ll write another one for you.”

Yeah. You know that’s the trick. That was recommended to me by my representation and really just asking around. I asked a lot of questions when I lived in New York. I was a very curious songwriter. And I think that’s how I ended up in certain circles and really learning a lot really quick while I was there. I was there for about three years and so I found myself in front of great songwriters like Julie Gold who wrote “From a Distance” and really picking their brains when it came to writing songs and the industry, how does that work and how does it work to your advantage. I took advantage of my time in New York to just really learn about the industry and meanwhile using the Atlantic name to get into a few big doors at the same time. So I got a chance to not work with but talk with Barry Eastman, who was the producer for Anita Baker. You know it was really important for me to just talk to people. I’m a conversationalist so for me it was about learning. And that’s what I took a lot of those lessons that I learned during that period into my own songwriting and forming my own record label later. And my career now.
